title: The Bro Hug
hook: The hug between men is often a handshake that changed its mind: a grip, a pull, a bump of chests and two slaps on the back, over in a second.
why:
A generation ago, in many places, straight men rarely hugged each other outside sport and funerals. Now the brief, back-slapping embrace between male friends is so common that it has a name. It is a remarkable piece of improvised culture: a way for men to embrace each other while signalling, through its speed, its slaps and its stiffness, that the embrace is comradely and nothing more.

This chapter takes the bro hug seriously. It describes its forms, what the research says about how the form and length of an embrace change its meaning, what the slaps seem to do, what hugs do for the body and mood, how the rules are changing among younger men, how to read the opening and the release so that nobody is hugged who does not want to be, and what to do when a quick hug becomes something more, which happens at funerals and reunions and is one of the most important moments a man can share with a friend.

teach.p:
The bro hug comes in several forms, usually chosen without thought. The commonest begins as a handshake: right hands clasp, held between the chests, and the left arm reaches over the other man's shoulder for a brief pull and a slap or two on the back. The grip between the chests keeps the bodies apart even as they meet.

The A-frame hug leans in from the shoulders while keeping the hips well back, so that the two bodies form the shape of a letter A. The side hug, an arm across the shoulders while both face forward, is common in photographs and at celebrations. The full embrace, chest to chest with both arms around the other man, is the strongest form, and most men reserve it for moments that matter.

Details carry meaning. Heads usually go to the same side, often the left, and a collision of heads is a common source of awkward laughter. The number and force of the slaps vary from two light pats to a series of thumps. And the whole thing is usually brief, a second or two, with a clear ending: a final slap, a step back, a hand that stays on the shoulder for a moment.

The figures here are mid-embrace in the handshake form, right hands still clasped between them, left arms over each other's shoulders. It is a hug and a handshake at once, and that double nature is the point: closeness offered inside a frame that keeps it safe.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if men's hugs showed no regular forms. The forms described here are widely observed, though their names and their frequency vary between places and generations, and no systematic survey of them exists.

teach.h: Form and length change the meaning.
teach.p:
In 1999 Kory Floyd showed 164 people videos of two men embracing, varying the form of the embrace and how long it lasted. Both mattered. An embrace in which both people took an equal part was read differently from one in which one person did most of the holding, and longer embraces were seen as more intimate and suggested a closer relationship. People also judged how expected or appropriate the embrace was, and those judgments depended on form and duration too.

How long is a typical hug? In 2011 Emese Nagy analysed 188 spontaneous embraces between athletes, coaches and supporters at the 2008 Beijing Olympics, frame by frame. They lasted on average a little over three seconds, and the length did not depend on whether the people were men or women, or on their nationality. Nagy linked this to a broader finding that around three seconds is a basic window in which people experience a moment as one unit.

The bro hug is typically shorter than that, often under two seconds, which is part of how it keeps its comradely frame. A hug that lasts three seconds or more begins to say something more: grief, relief, reunion, love. Both men usually know this, which is why the length of a hug between men is so closely watched, and why holding on is such a strong signal.

The figures here are in a full embrace, chests close, one arm over the shoulder and one around the back. Held for a second, it is a greeting. Held for ten, it is something else entirely.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if the form and length of a hug made no difference to how observers read it. Floyd found that they did, though with staged videos rather than real embraces, and Nagy's average comes from one kind of emotional occasion.

teach.p:
The slaps on the back are the signature of the bro hug, and they have not been studied directly, so what follows is interpretation rather than finding. They seem to do several jobs at once. They set a rhythm, so that the hug has a beginning, a middle and an end that both men can follow. They add vigour, turning an embrace into something closer to a physical greeting between teammates. And they signal the end: the second or third slap usually means time to let go.

Many people also read the slaps as a frame that keeps the hug comradely, a way of embracing that says this is friendship, not anything more. Whether or not that was ever their purpose, they work as a shared code. Two men who both slap know that they are doing the same kind of hug.

The slaps can carry other messages too. Very hard thumps can be a quiet contest, a display of strength that turns the embrace into a test. A single slap, or none, often signals a softer, more serious hug. And slaps that continue while the other man is holding on, as if to hurry him, can feel like a refusal of what he is offering.

Read the slaps the way you would read a handshake's grip. Match their force and number. Soften them when the moment is serious. And when a man holds on, stop slapping. The figures here stand side by side, arms across each other's shoulders, hands resting flat. Not every embrace between men needs a percussion section.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if back slaps carried no meaning at all, or the same meaning in every hug. They have not been studied directly, so this block offers an interpretation to test against your own experience rather than a result.

teach.h: What hugs do for the body.
teach.p:
Hugs are not only symbols. In a study published in 2015, Sheldon Cohen, Denise Janicki-Deverts and their colleagues asked about 400 healthy adults each evening for two weeks whether they had been in conflict with anyone and whether they had been hugged. Then they exposed them to a common cold virus under quarantine. Conflict raised the risk of infection, but less so for people who felt well supported, and hugs accounted for about a third of that protective effect. Among those who became infected, people who had been hugged more often had less severe symptoms.

In a follow-up published in 2018, Michael Murphy, Janicki-Deverts and Cohen looked at mood in the same kind of data. On days when people had a conflict, being hugged was associated with a smaller drop in good mood and a smaller rise in bad mood. The association was the same for men as for women.

These studies measured hugs rather than assigning them, so they cannot prove that hugs caused the benefits; hugs may simply mark relationships that are supportive in other ways. The researchers were also careful to say that a hug from a boss or a stranger may not help at all. But the findings fit the chapter on touch in Part I: welcome touch from people we trust seems to do the body good, and men are not exempt.

The figures here hold each other in a full embrace. The evidence suggests that, between people who want it, this is not a sentimental gesture but a small act of care with measurable effects.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if people who were hugged more fared no better after conflict or infection. The studies found that they did, but the data are correlational, so hugs may be a sign of support rather than its cause.

teach.p:
The bro hug's own history shows how fast rules about men's touch can change. The sociologists Eric Anderson and Mark McCormack, whose work on homohysteria was described in the previous chapter, interviewed 40 male student athletes at a British university in a study published in 2015. Thirty-seven of them described cuddling with close male friends, lying together on a bed or a sofa, and most saw nothing unusual in it.

This was a small, particular group, and it would be wrong to treat it as a picture of all young men. But it fits what many people notice: younger men in many places hug more, longer and with less stiffness than their fathers did, and the bro hug, which once marked a boundary, is for some of them simply a hug.

At the same time, the old rules are alive in many families, workplaces, sports clubs and communities. A man may hug his friends freely and still freeze when his father opens his arms. The same embrace that is ordinary in a university changing room may be risky in a different town. Culture, religion and class all shape what is allowed, and the chapters of Part V return to them.

The figures here stand together from behind, one with an arm across the other's shoulders while he bows his head. Whether two men can stand like this without comment depends on where they are and who is watching. That is worth remembering both when you offer closeness and when you judge it.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if men's hugging habits had stayed the same across generations. Anderson and McCormack's work suggests change, but it is based on small, particular groups, and the pace of change differs widely between places.

teach.h: Read the opening and the release.
teach.p:
Because men's hugs are negotiated in a second, reading the opening matters. The chapter on greetings described the signs: arms lifting from the sides, a step that keeps coming, a handshake that turns into a pull. When you want to offer a hug, offer it in a way that can be declined: start with a handshake and let a slight pull show what you would welcome, so that the other man can stay at the handshake without embarrassment.

Not every man hugs, and the reasons deserve respect. Some autistic men find hugs overwhelming. Some men who have been hurt find being held frightening, as the chapter on trauma described. Some faiths limit touch, which Part V discusses. Some men simply do not like it. Watch for a locked elbow on the handshake, a body that stiffens, hips kept far back in an A-frame, a step away. Each says not today, and should be accepted at once.

The release matters as much as the opening. In a quick hug, the slaps and a step back mark the end, and both men let go at about the same moment. If you are still holding when the other man has let go, release immediately. If he is still holding when you are ready to stop, that is a different situation, and the next block deals with it.

The figures here shake hands. A handshake is always available as the place to stop. Offering a hug from there, rather than launching into one, is the most reliable way to make sure that every hug you give is wanted.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if men who did not want to be hugged showed no signs of it. Most do show signs, though some freeze rather than resist, which is why offering a hug in a way that can be declined matters more than reading the signs alone.

teach.h: When the hug becomes something more.
teach.p:
At a funeral, a hospital, a reunion after years apart or the news of a death, a man may go into a quick hug and not come out of it. He holds on. His breathing changes. He may begin to cry, often silently, his face hidden in your shoulder where nobody can see it. For many men, this is one of the very few places they will ever cry in front of another man.

What helps is simple and difficult. Stop the slaps. Let your hand rest flat on his back, still, or move it slowly. Stay where you are. Do not speak unless something short and true comes to you, such as “I've got you” or “I know.” Let him decide when it ends, and when he steps back, let him wipe his face without comment.

Afterwards, do not joke about it, and do not tell anyone else what happened. Most men will not mention it again. Some will, years later, and say that it was the moment they finally let go. The chapter on mourning together, at the end of this part, returns to these moments.

The figures here stand side by side from behind, one arm across the other's shoulders, his head bowed. Sometimes the hug comes after, and sometimes this is all that is possible. Either way, the rule is the same: stay, be still, and let him set the length. A man who has been held like that by a friend tends to remember it for the rest of his life.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if men who held on in a hug wanted to be released quickly or distracted. Most accounts suggest the opposite, but people differ, so watch for signs that he wants to step back, and let him.
teach.pullQuote: When a man holds on, stop the slaps. Stay still, and let him set the length.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Pulling him in when he offered a handshake
poseGallery.annotation: Start from the greeting he offers. A slight pull lets him choose a hug without your forcing one.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Hugging a man who is leaning away
poseGallery.annotation: Hips back, elbow locked, body turning: he is saying not today. A fist bump or a nod keeps the warmth without the hug.

poseGallery.doCaption: Staying still while he holds on
poseGallery.dontCaption: Slapping and releasing while he holds on
poseGallery.annotation: When a man holds on, the slaps should stop. Let your hand rest on his back and let him decide when it ends.

poseGallery.doCaption: A side hug, an arm across the shoulders
poseGallery.dontCaption: A full hug for a man who stiffens
poseGallery.annotation: Not every man wants a full embrace. A side hug, both facing forward, offers warmth with more room and an easy way out.

poseGallery.doCaption: A quick pull-in hug, nothing to explain
poseGallery.annotation: Jokes about men hugging teach boys and men to stop. Letting a hug be ordinary keeps the door open for the next one.

poseGallery.doCaption: A long hug, slaps stopped, held
poseGallery.dontCaption: A brisk handshake after five years apart
poseGallery.annotation: At a reunion, a funeral or a hard goodbye, a quick greeting can turn into something more. Let it, and wait for him to let go.

caseStudy:
Luke, twenty-nine, has two close friends from university, and he greets them in completely different ways. With Sam, it is always the same: a handshake pulled into a half hug, two slaps, a step back and a grin. With Dev, who is autistic and has said that hugs are too much for him, it is a fist bump, and has been for years.

In March, Sam's father dies suddenly. At the funeral, Sam comes over to Luke after the service. Luke goes into the usual greeting, hand out, pull, and his left hand rises for the first slap. But Sam does not step back. He holds on, and Luke feels his breath catch against his shoulder.

Luke's hand stops in the air. He has a half-second of panic, and then he lets his hand come down flat on Sam's back, and stays still. He says nothing. He can feel Sam shaking. Around them, people carry on talking. Luke looks at the wall over Sam's shoulder and waits.

It lasts perhaps twenty seconds. Then Sam steps back, rubs his face with the heel of his hand, and says, “Cheers, mate.” Luke nods. Dev, who has been standing a little way off, comes over and bumps Sam's fist, and Sam laughs for the first time that day.

Neither Sam nor Luke mentions the hug again for two years. Then, at Luke's wedding, Sam says in his speech that the best thing anyone did for him that year was to stand still in a church hall and let him cry. He does not say who.
observe: Notice the forms of hug you see between men this week: handshake pull-in, A-frame, side hug, full embrace.
Notice how long men's hugs last, and what happens when one lasts longer than usual.
Notice the slaps: how many, how hard, and whether they change with the occasion.
Notice a man who does not hug, and how other men adjust to him, or fail to.

drills.name: Hug Census
steps: List the men you hug, or who hug you, and the form each hug usually takes.
Note how long each usually lasts and how many slaps it includes.
Mark any man you would like to hug and do not, or who hugs you when you would rather he did not.
Write one sentence about what the list shows about your relationships.
variations: Do the census for women in your life too, and compare the forms and lengths of the hugs.
Ask one man on your list whether he would like the way you greet each other to change.

drills.name: The Declinable Offer
steps: Practise, with a willing friend who knows what you are doing, offering a hug from a handshake with a slight pull.
Ask him to decline it sometimes by keeping his elbow firm.
Practise letting go at once when he declines, with no change in your expression.
Swap roles, so that you feel how easy, or hard, it is to decline.
variations: Practise declining yourself, so that you know how it feels to keep your elbow firm and still be warm.
Practise the offer at a real greeting, such as a farewell, where a slight pull is natural.

drills.name: Count to Three
steps: Over the next week, notice the length of the hugs you give and receive.
In one hug with someone close, let it last a full three seconds rather than one.
Notice how it feels, and how the other person responds.
Write a few lines about the difference.
variations: Notice which of your hugs you end first, and whether you could let the other person end one this week.
Notice the hugs on a sports broadcast and count how long the ones after big moments last.

drills.name: The Still Hand
steps: Imagine a friend holding on to you in a hug at a funeral.
Write down what you would do with your hands, your breath and your voice.
Write the one short sentence you might say, or decide to say nothing.
Practise, alone, letting a slapping hand come to rest and stay still.
Write down how you would behave afterwards, so that he does not feel exposed.
variations: Ask someone who has been through a loss what helped most when people hugged them, and what did not.
Practise the still hand on a hug with a partner or a close friend, and ask how it felt.

quiz.q: A friend says that hugs are something women need and men can do without. What does the research described in this chapter suggest?
options: He is right; studies find that hugs do nothing at all for men
On conflict days, hugs went with less mood change in men and women alike
Hugs help men more than women, because men are hugged less often
He is right; hugs only matter between romantic partners anyway
quiz.explain: Murphy and colleagues found that on days with conflict, being hugged was associated with a smaller drop in good mood and a smaller rise in bad mood, with no difference between men and women. The data are correlational, but they give no support to the idea that men do not benefit.

quiz.q: What did Nagy find when she analysed embraces at the 2008 Olympics?
options: Men's hugs were far shorter than women's hugs at the Games
Hugs lasted about a minute when athletes had won a medal
Hugs lasted a little over three seconds on average, whoever was hugging
Hug length depended mainly on the nationality of the athletes
quiz.explain: The average embrace lasted a little over three seconds, and length did not depend on gender pairing or nationality. The bro hug's usual brevity is part of how it keeps its comradely frame.

quiz.q: What did Floyd's 1999 study of filmed embraces show?
options: The form and length of a hug changed how intimate observers judged it
Observers could not tell the difference between any two embraces
Only the age of the people hugging affected how the hug was judged
Longer hugs were always judged as less intimate than short ones
quiz.explain: Both the form of the embrace and its duration influenced how expected, how intimate and how appropriate it seemed, and what relationship observers inferred. Length and shape are part of a hug's message.

quiz.q: At his father's funeral, your friend goes into the usual quick hug and then holds on, his breathing uneven. What fits this chapter best?
options: Give two firm slaps on the back, so that he can pull himself together
Step back gently and ask him whether he would like to get some air
Say something light to break the tension for both of you
Stop slapping, rest your hand flat, stay still, and let him end it
quiz.explain: When a man holds on, he is not doing a quick hug any more. Stillness, a flat hand and patience let him use the moment; slaps and jokes push him back behind the frame.

quiz.q: What did Cohen and colleagues find about hugs and the common cold?
options: Hugs spread colds, so people who hugged more fell ill more often
Hugs explained about a third of the protective effect of support
Hugs had no link with infection once people were exposed to the virus
Only hugs from romantic partners were linked with any protection
quiz.explain: Conflict raised infection risk less among well-supported people, and hugs accounted for about a third of that protective effect. Among infected people, more frequent hugs went with milder symptoms, though the data are correlational.

quiz.q: At a leaving party, a colleague who never hugs offers you a handshake with his elbow firmly locked. You are a hugger. What should you do?
options: Pull him into a hug anyway, since it is a special occasion
Shake his hand warmly and add your thanks in words instead
Refuse the handshake and wait for him to offer you something warmer
Clap him hard on the shoulder so that he knows you care
quiz.explain: A locked elbow on a handshake is a clear sign that he does not want to be pulled closer. Match the greeting he offers and put the warmth into your words.

quiz.q: In Anderson and McCormack's 2015 interviews with forty British student athletes, how many described cuddling with close male friends?
options: Thirty-seven of the forty, most of whom saw nothing unusual in it
None of them, since cuddling between men was found to be unheard of
About half, though most of them said that they felt ashamed of it
Only the four who were not playing team sports at the university
quiz.explain: Thirty-seven of the forty described cuddling with close male friends, and most saw nothing unusual in it. It was a small, particular group, but it shows how quickly the rules about men's touch can change.

quiz.q: At a party, an old friend hugs you without slapping, and holds on well past the usual second or two. People are watching. What fits this chapter best?
options: Slap his back twice to end it, and make a joke so that nobody gets the wrong idea
Push him away gently and say loudly that he has clearly had too much to drink
Stay still a moment longer, then later ask quietly whether he is all right
Hold on even longer, so that everyone in the room can see how close you are
quiz.explain: A hug that lasts longer than usual, without slaps, is a change from baseline and often a sign of need. Staying still says I'm here, and a quiet question later lets him say what happened.

quiz.q: Someone says that research has proved hugs stop you catching colds. What does this chapter say?
options: It is right, since everyone who was hugged in the study stayed perfectly healthy
One study linked hugs to modest protection; it is not proof or a cure
It is wrong, since the study found that hugs made colds much more likely
It is right, but only if the hug lasts for more than twenty seconds
quiz.explain: Cohen and colleagues found that hugs accounted for part of the protective effect of social support against colds in one study of about four hundred people. It is suggestive, not a cure.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific hug with another man that you remember: one that felt good, one that went wrong, or one that became something more than a greeting. Describe its form, how long it lasted, what your hands did, and how it ended. What did it say about the relationship? Then think of a man in your life you would like to embrace differently, more or less, and describe what you would change and how you would make it easy for him to decline.
reflection.guidance: Be concrete about the movements: the grip, the pull, the slaps, the length, who let go first. If you have never been hugged by a man in a way that mattered, that is worth writing about too. Consider whether there is a man in your life, perhaps your father or a son, for whom a slightly longer hug would say something you have not said.

failureMode: The first failure is to hug a man who did not want to be hugged: pulling him in from a handshake he offered, or ignoring a locked elbow, stiffening or a step back. The second is to treat the bro hug's rules as fixed, missing both how fast they are changing among younger men and how strongly they still hold in other places. The third is to slap, joke or let go when a man holds on, pushing him back behind the frame at the one moment he stepped out of it. The fourth is to tell others about a hug in which a man cried. And the fifth is to dismiss hugs as something men do not need, when the evidence suggests that welcome touch from trusted people helps men's bodies and moods as much as anyone's.

moreCases.title: The goodbye at the airport
moreCases.scene:
Phil, fifty-six, drives his son Jamie, twenty-two, to the airport. Jamie is moving to Australia for two years on a work visa. At the departure gate, Jamie's mother hugs him for a long time and cries. Then it is Phil's turn. He steps forward, grips Jamie's right hand, pulls him into a quick A-frame hug, hips well back, and slaps his back three times, hard. "Look after yourself, son." He lets go after about a second and steps back, his hands going into his pockets.

Jamie had wanted more. He had been dreading this moment for weeks, and he had imagined his father holding on. As he walks through security, he looks back, and his father is already looking at his phone. On the plane, Jamie texts his sister that Dad could not even manage a proper hug.

In the car park, Phil sits in the driver's seat without starting the engine for twenty minutes. His wife sits beside him and says nothing.

Phil had rehearsed what he would say on the drive to the airport. He had planned to tell Jamie how proud he was. When the moment came, he could not trust his voice, so he said the only safe sentence he had and let the slaps do the rest.

Jamie's mother, standing beside them at the gate, saw Phil's hands shaking as he put them in his pockets. She said nothing to Jamie, because there was no time, and because she thought he would understand one day.
moreCases.misread:
Jamie read the quick hug, the hard slaps and the hands in pockets as a sign that his father did not feel much, or could not be bothered. He did not see what happened in the car park, and he read the form of the hug as a measure of the feeling behind it.

He also read his father's quick turn to his phone as indifference, when it may have been the only way Phil could stop himself watching his son walk away.

And because the hug was the last thing that happened before the gate, it took on more weight than the twenty years of fatherhood behind it. A goodbye can feel like a summary of a relationship, even when it is only one second of it.
moreCases.betterRead: The bro hug is, among other things, a way for men to embrace while signalling that the embrace is under control. For many men of Phil's generation, the speed and the slaps are not a sign of shallow feeling but a way of managing feeling that might otherwise overflow. Floyd's research found that longer embraces are read as more intimate, which is exactly why a man afraid of breaking down at a departure gate keeps his short. Phil's hands in his pockets and his twenty minutes in the car park told a different story from the hug. A better reading, for Jamie, would have weighed the whole of his father's behaviour, not one second of it. Jamie's sister, when she got his text, rang their father, and then told Jamie about the car park. Jamie rang his dad from Singapore. Phil did not mention the hug. He asked whether the food on the plane was any good, and his voice cracked on the second sentence. When Jamie came home two years later, his father held on for a long time.

moreCases.title: The hug that went on too long
moreCases.scene:
At a friend's thirtieth birthday party, Mike, thirty, is in the kitchen when his old friend Carl arrives. They have not seen each other for six months. Carl walks straight over and hugs him: not the usual pull-in and slaps, but a full hug, both arms, and he does not let go. Two seconds, three, four. Mike, aware of people in the kitchen, slaps Carl's back twice, as if to end it, and starts to step back. Carl holds on a moment longer, then lets go, laughs too loudly and says, "Good to see you, mate," and goes to get a drink.

Mike feels awkward. Someone in the kitchen makes a joke about the two of them getting a room. Mike laughs it off.

Later in the evening, he finds Carl alone in the garden. Carl tells him that his marriage has ended and that he has been living in a rented room for two months.

Carl had also looked thinner, Mike noticed afterwards, and had not brought a present, which was unlike him. At the time, Mike had been too busy managing the room to notice anything about his friend.

Carl's phone had buzzed twice in his pocket during the hug, and he had ignored it. Mike noticed that later too, when Carl finally checked it in the garden, read a message and put the phone away again without replying, his jaw tight.
moreCases.misread:
Mike read the long hug through the room around him: unusual, slightly embarrassing, something to end before anyone made a joke. He did not read Carl, whose hug said that something had happened.

The joke in the kitchen mattered too. It confirmed Mike's fear that the hug looked odd, and it made the next step, asking Carl whether he was all right, feel even harder.

He also treated the joke in the kitchen as the most important reaction in the room, when the most important reaction was Carl's, and Carl had not laughed.
moreCases.betterRead:
A hug that lasts longer than the usual second or two, between two men who normally keep it brief, is a change from baseline, and changes are informative. Nagy's analysis of embraces between athletes found that hugs typically lasted around three seconds; Carl's went well past the point where the slaps usually end it, without slaps of his own. The rivals include drink, excitement at a reunion and, often, need. Mike's two slaps were the bro hug's signal to finish, and they told Carl that the moment was over before he was ready. A better reading would have noticed that Carl was not slapping, and stayed still for another second or two. That alone would have said, "I'm here." Afterwards, a quiet "You all right, mate?" would have opened the door that Carl had to open himself in the garden. Mike told him he was sorry about the kitchen. Carl said he had not noticed, which neither of them believed. They talked until two in the morning.

He also made a point, at the next few gatherings, of greeting Carl with a long, still hug, so that Carl would not have to start it himself.

moreCases.title: The man who did not hug
moreCases.scene:
Ollie, twenty-six, plays in a Sunday football team. After a win, the team hugs and celebrates in the changing room. Ollie, who is autistic, finds unexpected hugs overwhelming: the pressure, the noise, the smell of other people, the loss of control over his own body. He has learned to stand slightly apart after a goal and offer high fives instead. Most of the team know and are fine with it.

A new player, Jordan, joins in the autumn. After Ollie scores the winning goal, Jordan runs over and wraps him in a bear hug from behind, lifting him off his feet. Ollie goes rigid, his arms pinned, his face tight, and when Jordan puts him down, he walks to the corner of the changing room and sits with his head down. Jordan laughs and says, "What's up with him? It's just a hug!" A couple of others laugh.

The captain, Asif, who has played with Ollie for three years, sees Ollie's hands pressed hard against his knees.

Ollie has also been bear-hugged before, at a wedding, and had to leave the reception for an hour to recover. He has never told anyone on the team about it.

Ollie had told the previous captain about his preference in his first week, privately, and the team had simply absorbed it. Nobody had thought to tell Jordan, because it had stopped being something anybody thought about.
moreCases.misread:
Jordan read Ollie's rigidity and withdrawal as rudeness or oddness, because to him a hug after a goal is the most natural thing in the world. The players who laughed read it the same way.

And Jordan's "It's just a hug!" carried an assumption common to people who like hugs: that a hug is always a gift, and that refusing one is refusing friendship.

The laughter from the others mattered as much as Jordan's comment. It turned Ollie's distress into a joke at his expense, in the place where he had felt most at home.
moreCases.betterRead:
Not every man hugs, and the reasons deserve respect. Some autistic men find hugs overwhelming; some men have injuries, histories of abuse or simply strong preferences. A hug from behind, with no warning and no way to decline, removes every bit of the control that makes touch bearable for someone like Ollie. His rigid body, his pinned arms and his retreat to the corner were signs of overload, not of coldness. Asif's better response was to make room for the difference without making a scene. He told Jordan, quietly, that Ollie did not do hugs and that high fives were his thing. He went over to Ollie, sat a little way off, and said, "Great goal. Take your time." After a few minutes, Ollie came back. Jordan, a little embarrassed, held out his hand for a high five, and Ollie gave him one. After the next goal Ollie scored, Jordan got there first, palm up.

Asif also mentioned to the whole team, at the next training session, that some players did not like being grabbed after goals and that a high five was always fine, without naming Ollie.

moreCases.title: The grandfather who learned
moreCases.scene:
Stan, seventy-eight, has never hugged his sons. He shook their hands on their wedding days and patted their shoulders at their mother's funeral. It is simply not something he does. His grandson, Leo, nineteen, hugs everyone: his friends, his father, his uncles. When Leo leaves for university, he walks up to Stan in the hallway and hugs him, a proper hug, arms round his shoulders.

Stan goes stiff. His arms stay at his sides for a moment. Then, awkwardly, one hand comes up and pats Leo's back, twice, the way he pats the dog. Leo lets go and grins, and says, "See you at Christmas, Grandad."

Stan's son, Ray, Leo's father, watches from the kitchen door. He feels something complicated: a flash of envy, and something like grief.

Ray remembers clearly the day he went off to university himself, at eighteen, and his father shaking his hand at the station and saying, "Well, then." He had thought nothing of it at the time. Watching Leo, he thinks about it for the rest of the day.

Stan's wife died four years ago. Since then, nobody has touched him much at all, apart from the doctor and the barber. Leo's hug is the first in months, and it takes Stan the rest of the afternoon to stop thinking about it.
moreCases.misread:
Ray read his father's stiffness as the same coldness he had grown up with, and his own reaction as something to keep to himself. Stan, for his part, read the hug as something that happened to him rather than something he might take part in.

Leo, for his part, read the stiffness and pats as perfectly normal, which may be why he hugged his grandfather without hesitation. He had no history with the old rules to make the moment heavy.

Stan himself may also have misread the hug: as something done to an old man, rather than something offered to a grandfather who was loved.
moreCases.betterRead:
Anderson and McCormack's research describes younger men in some places being far more comfortable with affection between men than earlier generations, and families often show the change across three generations in a single hallway. Stan's stiffness was not necessarily coldness. It was the body of a man raised under stricter rules, meeting a gesture he had never learned. The pats on Leo's back, awkward as they were, were a move towards the hug, not away from it. Ray's better response, later that day, was to say something. He told his father that Leo hugged everyone, and that he wished he and Stan had done more of it. Stan said nothing for a long while, then said that his own father had never even shaken his hand. At Christmas, when Leo hugged him, Stan put both arms round him. When Ray arrived, an hour later, Stan stood up and, stiffly and briefly, hugged him too.

Leo, when his father told him about it later, said he had no idea his grandad had never hugged anyone. He started ringing Stan on Sundays.

workedReading.title: The reunion at arrivals
workedReading.scene:
Ade, forty-one, waits at the arrivals gate at Heathrow for his younger brother, Femi, who has been working in Lagos for five years. They have spoken on the phone most weeks, but they have not been in the same room since their mother's funeral. When Femi comes through the doors, pushing a trolley, he sees Ade and stops. His face changes. He leaves the trolley and walks straight towards Ade, faster than he needs to, his arms lifting from his sides.

Femi's last visit, for their mother's funeral, was a blur of arrangements. He flew in for three days and left the morning after. The two brothers hugged at the airport then too, quickly, both of them exhausted. Ade has thought about that hug often.

Ade has been thinking about this moment for days. He has wondered whether Femi will look older, whether they will know what to say to each other, and whether the five years have made them strangers.

steps.label: Read the opening
steps.text:
Ade reads the approach: a step that keeps coming, arms lifting from the sides, a trolley abandoned. This is not an offer of a handshake or a quick pull-in. It is an offer of a full hug. Ade opens his own arms to match it, rather than putting out his hand, which would turn the moment into a negotiation.

He also notices that he had expected a handshake. They are not huggers, as brothers. Femi's approach is a change from baseline, which tells Ade that this greeting will mean more than usual.

He also takes a step forward to meet Femi, rather than waiting for him to arrive. Closing the last metre yourself tells the other person that the hug is wanted, not merely allowed.

steps.label: Let the form follow him
steps.text:
They meet in a full hug, both arms. Ade starts the usual rhythm: one slap on Femi's back, then a second. Femi does not slap back. His arms tighten. Ade notices the absence of slaps on Femi's side and lets his own hand stop.

He also notices that his own slaps came automatically, before he had decided anything. The habit is strong, and it took an absence on Femi's side to make him notice it.

He also lets his arms wrap more fully than he usually would, matching the strength of Femi's hold, so that the hug feels shared rather than one-sided, which Floyd's research suggests changes how an embrace is read.

steps.label: Notice the length
steps.text:
One second, two, three. The usual bro hug would have ended by now. Femi's hold does not loosen. Ade feels his brother's breath catch against his shoulder, and then the small, uneven shudders of someone trying not to cry. He notes that this has stopped being a greeting and become something else.

He also notices that Femi's grip on his shoulder blades is tight, his fingers pressing in. That is the hold of someone holding on, not someone greeting.

He also reminds himself that a man crying in an airport has had a long journey in more ways than one. Whatever is coming out has probably been held for a long time.

steps.label: Make the hand still
steps.text:
Ade lets his hand rest flat on Femi's back, still. He does not slap, rub or pat. He breathes slowly, so that Femi can feel it. He does not say anything. People are walking round them with trolleys, and Ade turns them both slightly, so that Femi's face is towards the wall and away from the crowd.

He also lowers his own head slightly, so that his cheek is against the side of Femi's head. It is not something he planned. It happens, and it makes the hug feel more like shelter.

He also keeps his own face calm and his eyes on the wall behind Femi, so that anyone looking at them sees only two men hugging, not a moment that needs explaining.

steps.label: Wait for his release
steps.text:
Ade does not let go first. He waits until Femi's arms loosen of their own accord, which takes nearly half a minute. When Femi steps back, his eyes are red, and he laughs and wipes them with the back of his hand, and says, "Sorry, man. Long flight."

He also lets go a fraction of a second after Femi does, so that Femi is not the one left reaching. A gentle release, on the other person's cue, is part of a good hug.

He also notices that he wants to say something reassuring, such as "It's all right," and decides against it. Femi has not said anything is wrong, and the stillness says enough.

steps.label: Make the afterwards ordinary
steps.text:
Ade says, "It's good to see you," and goes to fetch the trolley. He does not mention the tears or ask what is wrong. In the car, he asks about the flight and the food, and lets Femi lead the conversation. Making the moment afterwards feel ordinary tells Femi that what happened at arrivals does not need explaining.

He also hands Femi a packet of tissues from his coat pocket without looking at him, which he had put there that morning, half knowing why.

He also suggests they stop for a coffee before the drive, which gives Femi a few minutes to settle in an ordinary place, with something to hold and something to look at.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text:
On the drive home, past the cemetery where their mother is buried, Femi asks whether they could stop there tomorrow. Ade says of course. At the grave the next day, Femi tells him that he had not been able to come back for the stone-laying and had felt ashamed of it for years. Ade tells him he never minded. Ade notes, afterwards, that the hug at arrivals said more than five years of phone calls, and that the most important thing he did in it was to stop slapping.

He also notes that he had very nearly offered a handshake when Femi came through the doors, because that was their habit. If he had, the whole visit might have started differently.

Femi tells him, on the last day of his visit, that the hug at arrivals was the first time he had cried since the funeral. Ade says nothing about it, and hugs him at departures, longer this time, without a single slap.

moreFailures.title: Hugging a man who did not want it
moreFailures.body:
Men's hugs are negotiated in a fraction of a second, and it is easy to override someone who was offering something less. A handshake pulled into a hug the other man did not offer, a hug from behind with no warning, a hug that ignores a locked elbow or a step back: each takes away his choice. For many men this is merely awkward, but for some, autistic men, men with injuries, men with histories of abuse, it can be overwhelming or frightening. Read the opening, offer hugs in a way that can be declined, starting from a handshake with a slight pull, and accept the answer at once, with no change in your expression.

It also helps to remember that some men tolerate hugs they do not want because refusing feels rude. A stiff body, arms that stay down or a quick step back after the hug are signs worth noticing, and worth respecting next time.

It also helps to watch for the moment of decision in an approach. A man who hesitates, slows down or glances at your hands as he comes towards you may be wondering what you will offer. A clear, early handshake or open arms resolves it for both of you.

And when you are the one declining, a clear, warm alternative helps: a handshake offered early, with a smile, or a raised hand for a high five. It tells the other person what you would like instead, so that nobody is left hanging.

moreFailures.title: Treating the rules as fixed
moreFailures.body:
The bro hug's rules are changing, and they vary enormously between places, generations and groups. Some young men hug and cuddle their friends freely; some older men have never hugged another man. A rule that holds in one group, such as two slaps and let go, may feel cold in another and too much in a third. Treating your own group's rules as universal leads to misreadings in both directions: reading an older man's stiff hug as coldness, or reading a younger man's long hug as something it is not. Read the individual and the setting, not the rule.

It also helps to adjust within a single friendship. A man who hugs freely at a wedding may want only a nod at the pub, and a man who never hugs may want one at a funeral. The setting changes the rules as much as the person does.

It also helps to notice your own generation's rules and how they feel to people outside them. A younger man's casual hug can feel overwhelming to an older man; an older man's handshake can feel cold to a younger one. Neither is wrong.

It also helps to remember that the same man can change. A man who never hugged at thirty may hug readily at sixty, after a loss, an illness or a grandchild, and the people around him should let him.

moreFailures.title: Slapping and letting go when he holds on
moreFailures.body:
When a quick hug turns into something longer, most men's instinct is to end it: another slap, a joke, a step back. That instinct is about managing the moment, and it pushes the other man back into composure he may not be able to hold. If a man holds on, especially at a funeral, a hospital, a reunion or after bad news, stop the slaps. Let your hand rest still on his back. Breathe slowly. Shield his face from others if you can. Wait for him to let go first. Then make what follows ordinary, so that he does not feel he has to explain.

It also helps to know that the man who holds on may be embarrassed afterwards. Saying nothing about it, or saying only "Good to see you," lets him keep his dignity.

In families, the same applies. A father who holds on at his son's wedding, or a brother at a parent's funeral, may never have done it before, and how the other person responds can decide whether he ever does it again.

If you are not sure whether he is holding on or simply hugging longer than you expected, stay still for another second. If he loosens, he was finishing; if he does not, he needed it.

moreFailures.title: Mocking men who hug
moreFailures.body:
Jokes such as "Get a room" or "Steady on, lads" are the quickest way to end a hug and the surest way to teach anyone watching that hugs between men are suspect. They also make it harder for the man who needed the hug to ask for one again. The previous chapter described how this kind of policing passes on the old rules. If you see two men hugging, especially if one of them seems to need it, the kindest thing is to look away, say nothing, and, if someone else makes the joke, not to laugh.

Fathers have a particular influence here. A father who hugs his sons, and who does not mock other men for hugging, shows boys that affection between men is ordinary.

It also helps to model the alternative. Men who hug their friends openly, in front of other men, without slaps or jokes, make it easier for others to do the same.

And if you are the one who made the joke, it is never too late to undo it. "Sorry about that comment earlier, mate. Good to see you two" costs nothing and tells everyone the joke was the problem, not the hug.

questions.q: Why do men slap each other's backs when they hug?
questions.a:
Nobody has studied it directly, so the answers are interpretation rather than finding. The slaps seem to do several jobs: they set a rhythm, so that both men know when the hug will end; they add vigour, turning an embrace into something like a physical greeting between teammates; and they signal comradeship, which some men use to keep a hug from being read as romantic. The second or third slap usually means time to let go. Watching what happens to the slaps is one of the most useful things a reader can do: when they stop, or are not returned, the hug has usually become something more.

It also helps to notice your own slaps. Many men find, once they pay attention, that they slap harder or faster when they feel uncomfortable, and that the slaps are as much for them as for the other man.

It also helps to notice that slaps tend to be lighter between close friends and harder between men who are less comfortable with the hug. A hard, fast slap is often a sign of a man keeping the embrace at arm's length.

It also helps to know that the slaps can become a habit even in very close friendships, and that some men drop them only with one or two people. Noticing who you hug without slapping tells you something about who you trust most.

questions.q: How long should a hug last?
questions.a:
There is no correct length, but there are typical ones. Emese Nagy's analysis of embraces between athletes at the 2008 Olympics found that hugs lasted around three seconds on average. Many bro hugs are shorter, a second or so, ended by the slaps. Floyd's research found that longer embraces are read as more intimate. So the length of a hug is part of its meaning: a quick one says greeting, a longer one says something closer. In practice, let the other person's hold guide you. If he loosens, let go; if he holds on, stay.

It also helps to remember that a hug's length is shared. If you let go at one second and he was holding for three, he will feel the gap, so watch his hold as well as your own.

It also helps to remember that some cultures hug for much longer than others, and that a three-second hug may feel brief in some families and very long in others.

questions.q: Are hugs actually good for your health?
questions.a:
There is some evidence that they may help, though it should not be overstated. In Cohen and colleagues' 2015 study, people who felt more supported and were hugged more often were somewhat protected against the effects of stress on catching a cold, and those who were infected had milder symptoms if they had been hugged more. It was one study, of about four hundred people, and hugs were one part of a wider picture of social support. Hugs are not medicine. But the research fits what many people feel: that physical affection from someone you trust can make hard times a little easier.

It also helps to remember that touch is only helpful when it is welcome. An unwanted hug is not good for anyone's health, however well meant.

It also helps to remember that hugs can be part of a wider picture of support: being asked how you are, being listened to, being invited out. Hugs on their own, without the rest, do less.

Some people also find that a hug before a stressful event, such as an exam or an operation, steadies them. Offering one, in a way that can be declined, is a small kindness.

questions.q: What if I am not a hugger?
questions.a:
That is fine. Many men, and many women, prefer handshakes, fist bumps, a hand on the shoulder or no touch at all, and their reasons, from temperament to sensory sensitivities to past experiences, deserve respect. It can help to make your preference easy to read: offer a handshake or a fist bump clearly and early, so that others do not go in for a hug. With close friends, it can help to say it once: "I'm not much of a hugger, but it's good to see you." People who know your preference will adjust, and the friendship does not depend on the form of the greeting.

It also helps to have a warm alternative ready, such as a firm handshake with your other hand on his arm, which many men find carries much of what a hug carries without the closeness.

It may also help to notice what you do offer. A man who never hugs but always rings on birthdays, always turns up to help and always remembers names is showing affection in other ways, and those ways count.

It also helps to tell people when you would welcome a hug, if you are someone who usually does not. "I could do with a hug, to be honest" is one of the bravest and most useful sentences a man can say to a friend.

questions.q: How do I hug someone who starts to cry?
questions.a:
Stay. Stop any slaps or pats, and let your hand rest flat and still on his back, or move it slowly. Breathe slowly yourself. Do not speak unless something simple comes, such as "I've got you" or nothing at all. If you are in public, turn so that his face is shielded from others. Do not let go first; wait until his arms loosen. When he steps back, do not comment on the tears or ask what is wrong straight away. Make the next moment ordinary, such as fetching a drink or picking up his bag, and let him decide whether to talk.

Afterwards, it can help to check in a day or two later, briefly, without mentioning the tears: "Good to see you the other day. How are you doing?"

It also helps to know that men who cry in a hug often feel embarrassed for days. A short, warm message later, with no mention of the tears, can help them know the moment was safe.

It also helps to remember that you may be moved too. If your own eyes fill, that is fine. Two men crying in a hug are not making a scene; they are sharing something.

questions.q: Is it all right to hug a male colleague?
questions.a:
It depends on the setting, the relationship, the culture of the workplace and, above all, the other person. In some workplaces, hugs between colleagues at a leaving do or after good news are normal; in others they would be unwelcome. Power matters: a senior person's hug is hard to decline, as the chapter on greetings described. The safe approach is to let the other person set the level, to offer a hug only in a way that can easily be declined, such as a handshake with a slight pull, and never to insist. When in doubt, a warm handshake and a few kind words do the same work.

It also helps to watch how the workplace greets people at moments that matter, such as a colleague returning from bereavement leave. A quiet word and a handshake, or a hug if the person clearly wants one, is often the most valued part of their first day back.

It also helps to watch for colleagues who hold back. Someone who never joins in group hugs may simply not want to, and making it easy to stay out, without comment, is part of a good team culture.

watch.title: I Love You, Man: Trailer
watch.notice: A man with no close male friends sets out to make one. Watch the awkward greetings, the hugs that do not quite work, and how much male friendship is negotiated through the body.

reviewPrompt: This week, read the opening of every hug you are offered, match it, and in one hug with someone close, let it last a full three seconds.
